## 0. The setting, made explicit

The statement to be proved is Lemma 3 of the theorem *Existence and Uniqueness of Direct Limit of Sequence of Groups*; it refers to objects ($G_\infty$, $H$, the $h_n$, the classes $[(x_n,n)]$) introduced in that theorem. I therefore first write out the standing data and conventions in full, so that the proof below is self-contained. Throughout, $\mathbb N = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$, although nothing depends on where the indexing begins.

**(D1)** A sequence of groups $\langle G_n\rangle_{n\in\mathbb N}$ together with group homomorphisms $f_n : G_n \to G_{n+1}$ (a direct system over $\mathbb N$).

**(D2)** For $n \le m$, the *transition map* $f_{nm} : G_n \to G_m$, defined recursively by
$$f_{nn} := \operatorname{id}_{G_n},\qquad f_{n,m+1} := f_m \circ f_{nm}\quad (m \ge n).$$

**(D3)** The disjoint union
$$S := \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb N} G_n \times \{n\} = \bigl\{(x,n) : n \in \mathbb N,\ x \in G_n\bigr\},$$
equipped with the relation
$$(x,n) \sim (y,m) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists\, k \ge \max\{n,m\} \ \text{ such that } \ f_{nk}(x) = f_{mk}(y).$$

**(D4)** The direct limit $G_\infty := S/{\sim}$, whose elements are the $\sim$-classes $[(x,n)]$, with the operation
$$[(x,n)]\cdot[(y,m)] := \bigl[\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\,f_{mk}(y),\ k\bigr)\bigr]\qquad\text{for any } k \ge \max\{n,m\},$$
and the canonical maps $g_n : G_n \to G_\infty$, $x \mapsto [(x,n)]$.

**(D5)** A group $H$ and group homomorphisms $h_n : G_n \to H$ that are *compatible with the $f_n$*:
$$h_{n+1}\circ f_n = h_n \qquad\text{for all } n \in \mathbb N.$$

Condition (D5) is the hypothesis under which the map $h_\infty$ is introduced in the parent theorem (it is the hypothesis of the universal property of the direct limit). It is not merely convenient: Remark 2 at the end shows that (D5) is *equivalent* to the conclusion of the lemma, so no proof of the lemma is possible without it.

> **Lemma 3.** Let $h_\infty : G_\infty \to H$ be given by $[(x_n,n)] \mapsto h_n(x_n)$. Then $h_\infty$ is a well-defined mapping and a group homomorphism.

Sections 1 and 2 record, with proofs, the facts about (D2)–(D4) used in Section 3 (these are the contents of Lemmas 1 and 2 of the parent theorem); the reader who grants them may go directly to Section 3, which is the proof proper. Nothing beyond the properties (D1)–(D5) as displayed above is used anywhere.

## 1. Elementary properties of the transition maps

**(A1)** *For all $n \le m$, the map $f_{nm}$ is a group homomorphism.*

*Proof.* Fix $n$ and induct on $m \ge n$. For $m = n$, $f_{nn} = \operatorname{id}_{G_n}$ is a group homomorphism. If $f_{nm}$ is a group homomorphism, then $f_{n,m+1} = f_m \circ f_{nm}$ is a composite of group homomorphisms, hence a group homomorphism. $\square$

**(A2)** *For all $n \le m \le k$ we have $f_{mk}\circ f_{nm} = f_{nk}$.*

*Proof.* Fix $n \le m$ and induct on $k \ge m$. For $k = m$: $f_{mm}\circ f_{nm} = \operatorname{id}_{G_m}\circ f_{nm} = f_{nm}$. If $f_{mk}\circ f_{nm} = f_{nk}$ for some $k \ge m$, then, using (D2) twice,
$$f_{m,k+1}\circ f_{nm} = (f_k \circ f_{mk})\circ f_{nm} = f_k \circ (f_{mk}\circ f_{nm}) = f_k \circ f_{nk} = f_{n,k+1}. \qquad\square$$

**(A3)** *For all $n \le m$ we have $h_m \circ f_{nm} = h_n$.*

*Proof.* Fix $n$ and induct on $m \ge n$. For $m = n$: $h_n \circ \operatorname{id}_{G_n} = h_n$. If $h_m \circ f_{nm} = h_n$ for some $m \ge n$, then by (D2) and (D5),
$$h_{m+1}\circ f_{n,m+1} = h_{m+1}\circ (f_m \circ f_{nm}) = (h_{m+1}\circ f_m)\circ f_{nm} = h_m \circ f_{nm} = h_n. \qquad\square$$

## 2. $G_\infty$ is a group (the content of Lemmas 1 and 2)

### 2.1 $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $S$

*Reflexivity.* Given $(x,n) \in S$, take $k := n \ge \max\{n,n\}$; then $f_{nn}(x) = f_{nn}(x)$, so $(x,n)\sim(x,n)$.

*Symmetry.* The defining condition is symmetric in $(x,n)$ and $(y,m)$, since $\max\{n,m\}=\max\{m,n\}$ and equality in $G_k$ is symmetric.

*Transitivity.* Suppose $(x,n)\sim(y,m)$ and $(y,m)\sim(z,p)$: choose $k \ge \max\{n,m\}$ with $f_{nk}(x) = f_{mk}(y)$, and $l \ge \max\{m,p\}$ with $f_{ml}(y) = f_{pl}(z)$. Put $q := \max\{k,l\}$. Then $q \ge k \ge n$, $q \ge k \ge m$, $q \ge l \ge m$ and $q \ge l \ge p$, so every transition map written below is defined. By (A2),
$$f_{nq}(x) = f_{kq}\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\bigr) = f_{kq}\bigl(f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = f_{mq}(y),$$
$$f_{mq}(y) = f_{lq}\bigl(f_{ml}(y)\bigr) = f_{lq}\bigl(f_{pl}(z)\bigr) = f_{pq}(z).$$
Hence $f_{nq}(x) = f_{pq}(z)$ with $q \ge \max\{n,p\}$, i.e. $(x,n)\sim(z,p)$. $\square$

Consequently the classes $[(x,n)]$ are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover $S$; in particular every element of $G_\infty$ is of the form $[(x,n)]$ for some $(x,n)\in S$, and
$$[(x,n)] = [(y,m)] \iff (x,n)\sim(y,m). \tag{$\ast$}$$

### 2.2 The operation in (D4) is well-defined

**Claim.** *Let $(x,n)\sim(x',n')$ and $(y,m)\sim(y',m')$, let $k \ge \max\{n,m\}$ and $k' \ge \max\{n',m'\}$. Then*
$$\bigl(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y),\,k\bigr) \sim \bigl(f_{n'k'}(x')f_{m'k'}(y'),\,k'\bigr).$$

*Proof.* Choose $a \ge \max\{n,n'\}$ with $f_{na}(x) = f_{n'a}(x')$, and $b \ge \max\{m,m'\}$ with $f_{mb}(y) = f_{m'b}(y')$. Put $q := \max\{a,b,k,k'\}$, so that $q \ge k \ge n,m$ and $q \ge k' \ge n',m'$ and $q\ge a,b$. Since $f_{kq}$ is a group homomorphism by (A1), and using (A2),
$$f_{kq}\bigl(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = f_{kq}\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\bigr)\cdot f_{kq}\bigl(f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = f_{nq}(x)\cdot f_{mq}(y).$$
Again by (A2), $f_{nq}(x) = f_{aq}\bigl(f_{na}(x)\bigr) = f_{aq}\bigl(f_{n'a}(x')\bigr) = f_{n'q}(x')$, and in the same way $f_{mq}(y) = f_{m'q}(y')$. The identical computation with the primed data gives
$$f_{k'q}\bigl(f_{n'k'}(x')f_{m'k'}(y')\bigr) = f_{n'q}(x')\cdot f_{m'q}(y').$$
The two right-hand sides are equal, and $q \ge \max\{k,k'\}$, which is exactly the assertion. $\square$

Taking $(x',n')=(x,n)$ and $(y',m')=(y,m)$ (with $k \ne k'$ allowed) shows that the right-hand side of (D4) is independent of the choice of $k$; the general case shows it is independent of the choice of representatives. Together with $(\ast)$ this shows that (D4) defines a binary operation $G_\infty \times G_\infty \to G_\infty$.

### 2.3 $G_\infty$ is a group

Let $a = [(x,n)]$, $b = [(y,m)]$, $c = [(z,p)]$ and put $k := \max\{n,m,p\}$.

*Associativity.* Since $k \ge \max\{n,m\}$ we have $ab = [(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y),k)]$, and since $k \ge \max\{k,p\}$ and $f_{kk}=\operatorname{id}_{G_k}$,
$$(ab)c = \bigl[\bigl(f_{kk}(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y))\cdot f_{pk}(z),\,k\bigr)\bigr] = \bigl[\bigl(\bigl(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y)\bigr)f_{pk}(z),\,k\bigr)\bigr].$$
Symmetrically, $bc = [(f_{mk}(y)f_{pk}(z),k)]$ and
$$a(bc) = \bigl[\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\cdot\bigl(f_{mk}(y)f_{pk}(z)\bigr),\,k\bigr)\bigr].$$
The two first coordinates are equal by associativity in the group $G_k$, so $(ab)c = a(bc)$.

*Identity.* Each $f_{nm}$ is a group homomorphism (A1), so $f_{nm}(e_{G_n}) = e_{G_m}$; hence for any $n,m$, taking $k=\max\{n,m\}$ we get $f_{nk}(e_{G_n}) = e_{G_k} = f_{mk}(e_{G_m})$, i.e. $(e_{G_n},n)\sim(e_{G_m},m)$. So the class $e := [(e_{G_n},n)]$ is independent of $n$. For $a = [(x,n)]$, taking $k = n$ in (D4),
$$a\cdot e = [(x\,e_{G_n},n)] = a, \qquad e\cdot a = [(e_{G_n}\,x,n)] = a.$$

*Inverses.* For $a = [(x,n)]$, taking $k=n$ in (D4),
$$a\cdot[(x^{-1},n)] = [(x x^{-1},n)] = [(e_{G_n},n)] = e,$$
and likewise $[(x^{-1},n)]\cdot a = e$.

Hence $G_\infty$ is a group. $\square$

## 3. Proof of Lemma 3

### 3.1 $h_\infty$ is a well-defined mapping

Consider the relation
$$\mathcal R := \bigl\{\bigl([(x,n)],\,h_n(x)\bigr) : (x,n) \in S \bigr\} \subseteq G_\infty \times H .$$
The assertion that $h_\infty : [(x_n,n)] \mapsto h_n(x_n)$ is a well-defined mapping from $G_\infty$ to $H$ is precisely the assertion that $\mathcal R$ is left-total and single-valued (many-to-one) as a relation from $G_\infty$ to $H$.

*Left-totality (every class receives at least one value, lying in $H$).* By §2.1 every element of $G_\infty$ is of the form $[(x,n)]$ for some $(x,n) \in S$, hence is the first coordinate of an element of $\mathcal R$. Moreover $h_n : G_n \to H$, so $h_n(x) \in H$; the codomain is therefore correct.

*Single-valuedness (the value does not depend on the representative).* Suppose $\bigl([(x,n)],u\bigr) \in \mathcal R$ and $\bigl([(y,m)],v\bigr) \in \mathcal R$ with $[(x,n)] = [(y,m)]$, where $u = h_n(x)$ and $v = h_m(y)$. By $(\ast)$ we have $(x,n)\sim(y,m)$, so by (D3) there is $k \ge \max\{n,m\}$ with
$$f_{nk}(x) = f_{mk}(y).$$
Since $n \le k$ and $m \le k$, property (A3) applies to both indices, and
$$u = h_n(x) = \bigl(h_k \circ f_{nk}\bigr)(x) = h_k\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\bigr) = h_k\bigl(f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = \bigl(h_k \circ f_{mk}\bigr)(y) = h_m(y) = v .$$

Thus $\mathcal R$ is a mapping: $h_\infty : G_\infty \to H$ is well-defined, and it satisfies
$$h_\infty\bigl([(x,n)]\bigr) = h_n(x) \qquad \text{for every } (x,n) \in S. \tag{$\dagger$}$$

### 3.2 $h_\infty$ is a group homomorphism

$G_\infty$ is a group (§2.3) and $H$ is a group (D5), so it remains to verify that $h_\infty$ preserves the operations.

Let $a, b \in G_\infty$ be arbitrary. By §2.1 we may write $a = [(x,n)]$ and $b = [(y,m)]$ with $(x,n),(y,m) \in S$. Put $k := \max\{n,m\}$. By (D4) (legitimate by §2.2),
$$ab = \bigl[\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\,f_{mk}(y),\,k\bigr)\bigr],$$
where $f_{nk}(x)\,f_{mk}(y)$ is a product in $G_k$, so that $\bigl(f_{nk}(x)f_{mk}(y),k\bigr) \in S$. Applying $(\dagger)$ to this representative, then using that $h_k$ is a group homomorphism, then (A3) for $n\le k$ and for $m\le k$:
$$h_\infty(ab) = h_k\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\,f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = h_k\bigl(f_{nk}(x)\bigr)\cdot h_k\bigl(f_{mk}(y)\bigr) = h_n(x)\cdot h_m(y) = h_\infty(a)\cdot h_\infty(b),$$
the last equality by $(\dagger)$ again. As $a,b \in G_\infty$ were arbitrary, $h_\infty$ is a group homomorphism. $\blacksquare$

## 4. Remarks

**Remark 1 (the compatibility property).** For every $n \in \mathbb N$ and $x \in G_n$, $(\dagger)$ gives $\bigl(h_\infty \circ g_n\bigr)(x) = h_\infty\bigl([(x,n)]\bigr) = h_n(x)$, so
$$h_\infty \circ g_n = h_n \qquad (n \in \mathbb N),$$
which is the property demanded of $h_\infty$ in the universal property of the direct limit. (Its *uniqueness* with this property is a separate statement, not claimed here.)

**Remark 2 (hypothesis (D5) is necessary as well as sufficient).** By (D2), $f_{n,n+1} = f_n \circ f_{nn} = f_n$, so for any $x \in G_n$, taking $k = n+1$ in (D3),
$$f_{n,n+1}(x) = f_n(x) = f_{n+1,n+1}\bigl(f_n(x)\bigr),$$
whence $(x,n) \sim \bigl(f_n(x),\,n+1\bigr)$ and therefore $[(x,n)] = [(f_n(x),n+1)]$. If the assignment $[(x_n,n)]\mapsto h_n(x_n)$ is single-valued, evaluating it at this one class in two ways forces
$$h_n(x) = h_{n+1}\bigl(f_n(x)\bigr).$$
So $h_{n+1}\circ f_n = h_n$ for all $n$ holds if and only if $h_\infty$ is well-defined; Lemma 3 is the "if" direction, and it would be false without (D5) whenever some $h_{n+1}\circ f_n \ne h_n$.
